D=/scr/wurgaft/auto-psych/agent_trees/88c1bd3cf1e5f7a8/repo/_runs/cell_1/experiment1/model_loop/iter_4/critique/test_stats
mkdir -p $D
cat << 'EOF' > $D/digit_reversal_target_yes_rate.py
# name: digit_reversal_target_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate on two-digit targets whose digit reversal (e.g. 21 for 12) is one of the examples, excluding targets that are themselves examples; observed above null means people use a digit-reversal similarity the model under-produces.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    rev = (t % 10) * 10 + (t // 10)
    two = (t >= 10) & (t <= 99) & (t % 10 != 0) & (rev != t)
    hit = (ex == rev[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    isex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    m = two & hit & ~isex
    return float(y[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > $D/double_half_target_yes_rate.py
# name: double_half_target_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate on non-example targets equal to double or half of some example; observed above null means people generalize via multiplicative neighbours more than the model predicts, below null means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    hit = ((ex * 2 == t[:, None]) | (ex == 2 * t[:, None])).any(axis=1)
    isex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    m = hit & ~isex
    return float(y[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > $D/late_minus_early_yes_rate.py
# name: late_minus_early_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate in the last third of trials (by trial_index) minus the first third; the model has no time dependence, so observed above null means people become more liberal over the session, below null more conservative.
def test_statistic(df):
    ti = df["trial_index"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    lo, hi = np.quantile(ti, [1/3, 2/3])
    a = y[ti <= lo]; b = y[ti >= hi]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(b.mean() - a.mean())
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > $D/single_example_distance_slope.py
# name: single_example_distance_slope
# description: Among one-example sets, Pearson correlation between yes and log(1+|target-example|); more negative observed than null means people show stronger numerical-magnitude similarity gradients than the model, less negative means weaker.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    one = ~s.str.contains(",").to_numpy()
    if one.sum() < 3:
        return 0.0
    x = pd.to_numeric(s[one], errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()[one]
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()[one]
    d = np.log1p(np.abs(t - x))
    ok = np.isfinite(d)
    d, y = d[ok], y[ok]
    if d.std() == 0 or y.std() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.corrcoef(d, y)[0, 1])
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > $D/just_outside_range_yes_rate.py
# name: just_outside_range_yes_rate
# description: Among multi-example sets, yes rate on targets lying 1-5 outside the examples' min-max range; observed above null means people extend ranges beyond the examples more than the model's interval hypotheses predict, below null means sharper edges.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.isfinite(ex).sum(axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    dist = np.where(t < lo, lo - t, np.where(t > hi, t - hi, 0.0))
    m = (n >= 2) & (dist >= 1) & (dist <= 5)
    return float(y[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > $D/parity_violation_yes_rate.py
# name: parity_violation_yes_rate
# description: Among sets of 2+ examples that are all even or all odd, yes rate on targets of the opposite parity; observed above null means people respect parity less than the model (too few false alarms in the model), below null means the model over-generalizes across parity.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    fin = np.isfinite(ex)
    n = fin.sum(axis=1)
    par = np.where(fin, np.mod(np.nan_to_num(ex), 2), np.nan)
    ev = np.nansum(par == 0, axis=1); od = np.nansum(par == 1, axis=1)
    alle = (n >= 2) & (ev == n); allo = (n >= 2) & (od == n)
    m = (alle & (t % 2 == 1)) | (allo & (t % 2 == 0))
    return float(y[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > $D/between_set_yes_rate_variance.py
# name: between_set_yes_rate_variance
# description: Variance across distinct number_sets of the per-set mean yes rate; observed above null means people's generalization breadth differs more sharply between sets (more all-or-none) than the model, below null means less set-specific.
def test_statistic(df):
    g = df.groupby(df["number_set"].astype(str))["rating"].mean()
    return float(np.var(g.to_numpy(dtype=float))) if len(g) > 1 else 0.0
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > $D/last_vs_first_example_proximity.py
# name: last_vs_first_example_proximity
# description: Among multi-example sets and non-example targets, yes rate when the target is numerically closer to the last-shown example minus when closer to the first-shown; the model is order-invariant, so a nonzero observed-vs-null gap means a recency (positive) or primacy (negative) effect.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    fin = np.isfinite(ex)
    n = fin.sum(axis=1)
    first = ex[:, 0]
    idx = np.clip(n - 1, 0, ex.shape[1] - 1)
    last = ex[np.arange(len(ex)), idx]
    isex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    df_ = np.abs(t - first); dl = np.abs(t - last)
    base = (n >= 2) & ~isex & (first != last)
    a = base & (dl < df_); b = base & (df_ < dl)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())
EOF
ls $D; cd /tmp && python3 -I -c "
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, math, glob, time
df=pd.read_csv('/scr/wurgaft/auto-psych/agent_trees/88c1bd3cf1e5f7a8/repo/_runs/cell_1/experiment1/model_loop/responses.csv')
print(df.shape)
for f in sorted(glob.glob('$D/*.py')):
    g={'np':np,'pd':pd,'math':math}; exec(open(f).read(),g); t=time.time()
    print(f.split('/')[-1], g['test_statistic'](df[['number_set','target','trial_index','rating']]), round(time.time()-t,3))
"

content.text:
I wrote all 8 test statistics to `iter_4/critique/test_stats/`. Last attempt's files were rejected for importing pandas. None of these files has an import line: they use only the `np`, `pd` and `math` the harness already provides. I ran each once on the observed data (2250 rows). Every one returned a finite number in under 20 ms. I didn't run the harness, so there are no p-values yet.

| Statistic | Observed | What it checks (the model has no mechanism for any of these) |
|---|---|---|
| `digit_reversal_target_yes_rate` | 0.373 | "Yes" rate when the target is an example with its digits reversed (21 for 12) |
| `double_half_target_yes_rate` | 0.305 | "Yes" rate when the target is double or half of an example |
| `just_outside_range_yes_rate` | 0.406 | "Yes" rate 1–5 beyond the examples' min–max, i.e. how sharp people treat range edges |
| `parity_violation_yes_rate` | 0.103 | "Yes" rate on odd targets after all-even examples, and on even targets after all-odd ones |
| `single_example_distance_slope` | −0.215 | With one example, how steeply "yes" falls off as the target gets numerically further away |
| `between_set_yes_rate_variance` | 0.065 | How much the average "yes" rate differs from one example set to another |
| `late_minus_early_yes_rate` | −0.140 | "Yes" rate in the last third of trials minus the first third |
| `last_vs_first_example_proximity` | −0.028 | "Yes" rate for targets nearer the last example shown vs nearer the first (recency or primacy) |

The early-to-late drop of 0.14 in "yes" rate looks big for a model with no time dependence. Treat that as a guess until the harness reports the p-values.

I also saved a memory note so the next critique round doesn't repeat the import mistake.
